newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD adopts communications encryption guidelines.
newsitem.headline: OECD adopts communications encryption guidelines.

text.p: The OECD agreed policy guidelines on Thursday on communications-scrambling technology, but steered clear of saying where the line should be drawn between privacy and eavesdropping on electronic commerce and the Internet.

They advise the 29 OECD governments to promote market-driven "encryption" software, protect the right to privacy and to avoid "unjustified obstacles" to international trade in a technology which is developing at breakneck speed.

The wording of the guidelines, a copy of which was supplied to Reuters, does not offer any explicit advice on how national governments should strike a balance between privacy rights and wiretapping in cyberspace by police and law enforcement bodies.

"They do not give all the answers but they are a major step in getting countries to promote policies which interact," said John Dryden, one of the key officials involved in the accord at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
"It's not possible to give definitive answers, because the (OECD) countries themselves do not have definitive answers," Dryden told Reuters.
The document was the result of consensus negotiations and the primary aim was to promote international coordination of policies which were only at fledgling stage in many countries.
"Governments want to encourage the use of cryptography for its data protection benefits and commercial applications," said the OECD statement announcing the agreement.
"But they are challenged to draft cryptography policies which balance the various interests at stake, including privacy, law enforcement, national security, technology development and commerce."

So far, the battle between promoting electronic commerce, protecting privacy and ensuring that law enforcement agencies can eavesdrop on modern communications has largely taken place in the United States.

Lobbies for privacy protection and other corporate interests are fighting U.S. restrictions which prevent companies exporting "encryption" technology unless they promise to include "recovery keys" which can be used to crack communications codes.

The OECD guidelines say the development of "encryption", or data-scrambling, technology should be market-driven and advise governments to avoid "unjustified obstacles to the international availability of cryptographic methods".

The development of such technology provides a useful way of protecting privacy, in terms of the indentity of individuals and the confidentiality of communications, as well as offering ways of minimising collection of personal data and securing ways of carrying out payments and transactions anonymously, they say.

"The fundamental rights of individuals to privacy, including secrecy of communications and the protection of personal data, should be respected in national cryptography policies and in the implementation and use of cryptographic methods," they say.
The guidelines are not binding on OECD member countries.

David Aaron, U.S. ambassador to the OECD, told reporters on the eve of the Thursday accord that Washington was working on liberalising policy but it was equally important to counter exploitation of coding technology by terrorist groups, child pornography networks or other illegal organisations.
But opponents argue that draft legislation is encouraging widespread use of recovery keys, or code crackers, to the extent that it effectively becomes a requirement.

Asked how the guidelines fitted with U.S. controls, Dryden said: "The (U.S.) export restrictions are not unjustified. They're justified by reasons of security. They are not justified by any attempt to gain economic advantage".

U.S. worries about "strong encryption" and the need to gain "lawful access" to coded communications for national security reasons and to fight criminal organisations were shared by other countries like France, he added.
